question_text: Differentiate between globular and fibrous proteins.

verification.note: Unit 13 (Biomolecules) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", printed chapter 10 "BIOMOLECULES", book pp.99-104; the book prints this question on book p.100 as VSAQ 11. page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Globular proteins
lines: The polypeptide chains are coiled round on
themselves to give a roughly spherical
steps.why: The shape and the solubility go together. A globular protein folds so that its water-attracting groups face outwards, which is why it dissolves; it can then travel in the blood and act as a hormone or an enzyme.
common_mistakes: Giving keratin or myosin as a globular protein. Both are fibrous.
Writing only the shape. The mark expects the shape, the solubility and an example.
steps.memory_tip: Globular means ball shaped, soluble, and it works in solution.
steps.margin_note: Three things per column: shape, solubility, example. Answer it as a table if there is room.

steps.label: Fibrous proteins

lines.text: Fibrous: thread-like and insoluble in water

lines: The polypeptide chains run parallel to one
another and are held together by hydrogen
steps.why: Parallel chains held alongside one another make a thread, and that shape is what a structural material must have. Insolubility follows from the same packing, and it is what makes these proteins useful in hair, nails, skin and muscle.
common_mistakes: Writing that fibrous proteins are soluble in water. They are insoluble; the globular ones dissolve.
Swapping the examples. Insulin and albumin are globular; keratin and myosin are fibrous.
steps.memory_tip: Fibrous means fibre: parallel chains, insoluble, structural.
steps.margin_note: A two-column table earns this quickly. Keep the same three rows in both columns.

insider_note: Answer this as a table with three rows: shape, solubility, example. The examples are the fastest marks and the easiest to swap by mistake.
